'''''Cymbopogon citratus''''', commonly known as '''West Indian lemon grass'''<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | access-date=February 28, 2025}}</ref> or simply '''lemon grass''',<ref name=PLANTS>{{PLANTS | symbol = CYCI | taxon = Cymbopogon citratus | accessdate = January 12, 2019 }}</ref> is a tropical [[plant]] native to [[South Asia]] and [[Maritime Southeast Asia]] and introduced to many tropical regions.<ref name=POWO>{{cite web | title = ''Cymbopogon citratus'' | work = [[Plants of the World Online]] | publisher = [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] | url = https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:396896-1 | access-date = March 4, 2019}}</ref>

''Cymbopogon citratus'' is often sold in stem form. While it can be grown in warmer temperate regions, it is not [[Hardiness (plants)|hardy]] to frost.

== Morphology ==
''Cymbopogon citratus'' is part of the grass family, [[Poaceae]]. They contain simple, bluish-green leaves with entire margins and are linear in shape. The blades tend to be 18–36 inches long. Like other grasses, the leaves also have parallel venation.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Shah|first1=Gagan|last2=Shri|first2=Richa|last3=Panchal|first3=Vivek|last4=Sharma|first4=Narender|last5=Singh|first5=Bharpur|last6=Mann|first6=AS|date=2011|title=Scientific basis for the therapeutic use of Cymbopogon citratus, stapf (Lemon grass)|url= |journal=Journal of Advanced Pharmaceutical Technology & Research|volume=2|issue=1|pages=3–8|doi=10.4103/2231-4040.79796|pmid=22171285|pmc=3217679|issn=2231-4040 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Distribution==
''Cymbopogon citratus'' is native to [[South Asia]] and [[Maritime Southeast Asia]] ([[Malesia]]). After [[World War I]], lemongrass was introduced to [[Madagascar]], [[South America]], and [[Central America]]. It has now been naturalized throughout the tropics and subtropics worldwide.<ref name="Oyen">{{cite web |last1=Oyen |first1=L.P.A. |title=''Cymbopogon citratus'' (PROSEA) |url=https://uses.plantnet-project.org/en/Cymbopogon_citratus_(PROSEA) |website=Pl@ntUse |access-date=30 June 2019}}</ref>

In its native range, ''Cymbopogon citratus'' is known as ''sereh'', ''serai'', or ''serai dapur'' in [[Indonesia]] and [[Malaysia]]; and ''tanglad'' (from [[Proto-Austronesian language|Proto-Austronesian]] *''Caŋelaj'' originally referring to ''[[Themeda gigantea]]'', a type of elephant grass<ref>{{cite web|url=https://acd.clld.org/cognatesets/32388#5/15.124/122.273|title=*Caŋelaj elephant grass, miscanthus grass: Themeda gigantea|last1=Blust|first1=Robert|last2=Trussel|first2=Stephen|website=Austronesian Comparative Dictionary|date=2010|publisher=Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology|access-date=8 November 2022}}</ref>), ''salai'', or ''balioko'' in the [[Philippines]].<ref name="Oyen"/> In [[Hmong language|the language]] of the [[Hmong people]], who are a diasporic people spread across Southeast Asia including Laos and Thailand, it is called {{lang|hmn|tauj dub}}.<ref name="Crum">{{cite thesis |last=Crum |first=Alexandra Hazel |date=2024 |title=Medicines, Metabolites, and Pigments in Caryophyllales and Beyond |url=https://www.yangya.org/publications.html |degree=Doctor of Philosophy |chapter= |publisher=University of Minnesota |docket= |oclc= |id={{ProQuest|31327584}} |access-date=October 30, 2024}}</ref>

==Culinary uses==
[[File:Lemongrass sold at a supermarket in the Philippines.jpg|thumb|Knots of ''C. citratus'' leaves sold at a supermarket in the [[Philippines]]]]
[[File:Tom yam kai ingredients.jpg|thumb|Ready-to-use bundles of lemon grass, galangal, kaffir lime leaves, and, for chicken tom yam, also turmeric, are sold at Thai markets.]]
''Cymbopogon citratus'' is abundant in the [[Philippines]] and [[Indonesia]] where it is known as ''tanglad'' or ''sereh'', respectively. Its fragrant leaves are traditionally used in cooking, particularly for ''[[lechon]]'' and roasted chicken.<ref name="tanglad">{{cite web|url=http://www.marketmanila.com/archives/tanglad-lemongrass|title=Tanglad / Lemongrass|date=August 21, 2006|publisher=Market Manila|access-date=July 27, 2011}}</ref>

The dried leaves can also be brewed into a tea, either alone or as a flavoring in other teas, imparting a flavor reminiscent of lemon juice, but with a mild sweetness without significant sourness or tartness.

In [[Sri Lanka]], lemongrass is known as ''sera'' (සේර). It is used as a herb in cooking, in addition to its use for the essential oils.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.srilankanspices.com/sl_spices_lemongrass.html |title=The Spice Council of Sri Lanka |website=www.srilankanspices.com |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110323024319/http://www.srilankanspices.com/sl_spices_lemongrass.html |archive-date=2011-03-23}}</ref>

Lemongrass in Thailand is called ''takhrai'' (ตะไคร้). It is the essential ingredient of ''[[tom yam]]'' and ''[[tom kha kai]]''. Fresh, thin slices of lemongrass stem are also used in the snack food [[Miang kham|miangpla]].

== Medicinal uses==
{{more medical citations needed|section|date=December 2015}}
The leaves of ''Cymbopogon citratus'' have been used in traditional medicine and are often found in herbal supplements and teas. Evidence of effective ''Cymbopogon citratus'' essential oil anti-protozoa activity against ''Leishmania amazonensis''.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Santin|first1=Marta Regina|last2=dos Santos|first2=Adriana Oliveira|last3=Nakamura|first3=Celso Vataru|last4=Dias Filho|first4=Benedito Prado|last5=Ferreira|first5=Izabel Cristina Piloto|last6=Ueda-Nakamura|first6=Tânia|date=2009|title=In vitro activity of the essential oil of Cymbopogon citratus and its major component (citral) on Leishmania amazonensis|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s00436-009-1578-7|journal=Parasitology Research|language=en|volume=105|issue=6|pages=1489–1496|doi=10.1007/s00436-009-1578-7|pmid=19669793|s2cid=22754248|issn=0932-0113|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

=== Chemical composition ===
Lemon grass oil contains 65–85% [[citral]] in addition to [[myrcene]], [[citronellal]], [[citronellol]], [[linalool]] and [[geraniol]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shaikh |first1=Mosma |last2=Suryawanshi |first2=Yogesh |last3=Digambar |first3=Mokat |title=Volatile Profiling and Essential Oil Yield of Cymbopogon citratus (DC.) Stapf Treated with Rhizosphere Fungi and Some Important Fertilizers |journal=Journal of Essential Oil Bearing Plants |date= 2019 |volume=22 |issue=2 |pages=477–483 |doi=10.1080/0972060X.2019.1613933|s2cid=191177588 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|author1=Baby P. Skaria|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=e68EbGOCayAC&pg=PA103|title=Aromatic Plants|author2=P.P. Joy|author3=Samuel Mathew|author4=Gracy Mathew|author5=Ancy Joseph|author6=Ragina Joseph|date=2007|publisher=New India Publishing Agency|isbn=9788189422455|volume=1|location=New Delhi, India|page=103}}</ref> Hydrosteam distillation, condensation, and cooling can be used to separate the oil from the water. The [[Herbal distillate|hydrosol]], as a [[by-product]] of the distillation process, is used for the production of skin care products such as lotions, creams, and facial cleansers. The main ingredients in these products are lemon grass oil and "negros oil" (mixture of lemon grass oil with [[virgin coconut oil]]) used in [[aromatherapy]].<ref>[http://business.inquirer.net/money/topstories/view/20080628-145358/Tanglad-goes-mainstream-yields-essential-oils Inquirer.net, ‘Tanglad’ goes mainstream, yields essential oils] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080629064405/http://business.inquirer.net/money/topstories/view/20080628-145358/Tanglad-goes-mainstream-yields-essential-oils|date=2008-06-29}}</ref>

[[Citronellol]] is an essential oil constituent from ''Cymbopogon citratus'', ''Cymbopogon winterianus'', and ''Lippia alba''. Citronellol has been shown to lower blood pressure in rats by a direct effect on the vascular smooth muscle leading to vasodilation.<ref>{{Cite journal|author=Bastos JF. Moreira IJ. Ribeiro TP. Medeiros IA. Antoniolli AR. De Sousa DP. Maree JE. Sibanyoni M.|date=2009|title=Treatment of oral thrush in HIV/AIDS patients with lemon juice and lemon grass (Cymbopogon citratus) and gentian violet|journal=Phytomedicine|volume=16|issue=2–3|pages=118–124|doi=10.1016/j.phymed.2008.07.015|pmid=19109001}}</ref>

=== Traditional medicinal use ===
In the [[folk medicine]] of the [[Krahô]] people of Brazil, it is believed to have anxiolytic, hypnotic, and anticonvulsant properties.<ref>{{Cite journal|vauthors=Blanco MM, Costa CA, Freire AO, Santos JG, Costa M |title=Neurobehavioral effect of essential oil of Cymbopogon citratus in mice |journal=Phytomedicine |volume=16 |issue=2–3 |pages=265–70 |date=March 2009 |pmid=17561386 |doi=10.1016/j.phymed.2007.04.007 }}</ref><ref>Rodrigues, Eliana & Carlini, E.A. (2006): Plants with possible psychoactive effects used by the Krahô Indians, Brazil. ''Revista Brasileira de Psiquiatria'' '''28'''(4): 277–282. [http://www.scielo.br/pdf/rbp/nahead/2282.pdf PDF fulltext] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200801113240/https://www.scielo.br/pdf/rbp/nahead/2282.pdf |date=2020-08-01 }} <!-- citation verified, see non-searchable table on last page --></ref>

In [[traditional medicine]] of [[India]] the leaves of the plant are used as [[stimulant]], [[sudorific]], antiperiodic, and [[anticatarrhal]], while the essential oil is used as [[carminative]], [[depressant]], [[analgesic]], antipyretic, antibacterial, and [[Antifungal medication|antifungal]] agent.

==Effect on insects==
[[File:Repellency of lemongrass oil against stable flies - Figure 2.tif|thumb|right|Video tracking of a [[stable fly]], demonstrating repellency of lemongrass oil 
<ref name="Baldacchino">{{cite journal |last1=Baldacchino |first1=Frédéric |last2=Tramut |first2=Coline |last3=Salem |first3=Ali |last4=Liénard |first4=Emmanuel |last5=Delétré |first5=Emilie |last6=Franc |first6=Michel |last7=Martin |first7=Thibaud |last8=Duvallet |first8=Gérard |last9=Jay-Robert|first9=Pierre |title=The repellency of lemongrass oil against stable flies, tested using video tracking |journal= Parasite |volume=20 |year=2013 |pages=21 |issn=1776-1042 |doi=10.1051/parasite/2013021  |doi-access=free|url= |pmid=23759542 |pmc=3718533}}</ref>]]

[[Beekeeper]]s sometimes use lemon grass oil in swarm traps to attract [[Swarming (honey bee)|swarms]]. Lemon grass oil has also been tested for its ability to repel the pestilent [[stable fly]],<ref name="Baldacchino" /> which bite domestic animals.

== Growing conditions ==

=== Light and Climate ===
Lemongrass (''Cymbopogon citratus'') thrives in full sun conditions, requiring at least 6 to 8 hours of sunlight per day. Exposure to supplemental ultraviolet-B (sUV-B) radiation has been shown to enhance both the yield and quality of essential oils.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Anggraeni |first1=Nenden Indrayati |last2=Hidayat |first2=Ika Wiani |last3=Rachman |first3=Saadah Diana |last4=Ersanda |date=2018 |title=Bioactivity of essential oil from lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus Stapf) as antioxidant agent |url=https://doi.org/10.1063/1.5021200 |journal=AIP Conference Proceedings |volume=1927 |page=030007 |publisher=Author(s) |doi=10.1063/1.5021200|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The optimal temperature range for cultivation is between 25 °C and 30 °C. The species is sensitive to low temperatures, and prolonged exposure to temperatures below 10 °C may result in plant mortality. The ideal annual rainfall ranges between 2,500 and 3,000 mm.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cymbopogon citratus Lemon Grass, Citronella grass PFAF Plant Database |url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Cymbopogon+citratus |access-date=2025-05-21 |website=pfaf.org}}</ref>

=== Soil condition ===
Well-drained sandy loam soil with a pH range of approximately 5.5 to 7.5 is considered optimal. Moderate soil fertility is sufficient, and the application of organic fertilizers during the early growth stage can promote tillering.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=BRAY |first=ROGER H. |date=August 1948 |title=Requirements for Successful Soil Tests |url=https://doi.org/10.1097/00010694-194808000-00001 |journal=Soil Science |volume=66 |issue=2 |pages=83–90 |doi=10.1097/00010694-194808000-00001 |issn=0038-075X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Propagation method ==

=== Division or Tillering ===
Lemongrass (''Cymbopogon citratus'') is primarily propagated through division or tillering, as seed propagation is inefficient due to its rare flowering and fruiting. Mature lemongrass clumps typically consist of 50 to 200 tillers. Propagation involves cutting the upper leaves and separating rooted divisions approximately 10 to 15 cm in length from the mother plant, which can then be directly planted in the field.<ref>{{Cite web |title=43-5 禾本科香藥草植物－檸檬香茅(lemon grass)(臺中區農業改良場) |url=https://www.tcdares.gov.tw/ws.php?id=1898 |access-date=2025-05-21 |website=www.tcdares.gov.tw}}</ref>

=== Tissue culture ===
An efficient in vitro mass propagation system for Cymbopogon citratus has been developed using both organogenesis and somatic embryogenesis. The study optimized conditions such as liquid culture media, plant growth regulators, and temporary immersion systems (TIS) to achieve high multiplication and rooting rates.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Teixeira da Silva |first1=Jaime A. |chapter=Somatic Embryogenesis in Two Orchid Genera (Cymbidium, Dendrobium) |date=2016 |title=In Vitro Embryogenesis in Higher Plants |volume=1359 |pages=371–386 |editor-last=Germana |editor-first=Maria Antonietta |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/protocol/10.1007/978-1-4939-3061-6_18 |access-date=2025-05-21 |place=New York, NY |publisher=Springer New York |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-1-4939-3061-6_18 |isbn=978-1-4939-3060-9 |last2=Winarto |first2=Budi |pmid=26619873 |editor2-last=Lambardi |editor2-first=Maurizio|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> This method offers a scalable and cost-effective approach for producing lemongrass plantlets, especially useful in medicinal and essential oil production industries.
